subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Smallholder Farmer
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Smallholder Farmer.

hook.text: About 80% of the world's coffee is grown by smallholder farmers with less than 5 hectares of land.

buildup.text: These families do everything by hand—planting, pruning, picking, and processing. It's exhausting, skilled labor.

discovery.text: Most smallholders sell raw cherries to a local buyer for whatever price is offered. Negotiation power is near zero.

twist.text: A farmer who grows exceptional coffee often earns the same as one growing average beans. The market doesn't differentiate.

climax.text: Young people in coffee regions are leaving farming for cities. The average coffee farmer's age keeps climbing.

punchline.text: 25 million families grow coffee. Most can barely live on it.

quiz.question: What percentage of coffee is grown by smallholder farmers?

details.summary: About 80 percent of the world's coffee is grown by smallholder farmers working plots under five hectares. These families often earn less than two dollars a day and face volatility in global prices beyond their control. Their livelihoods depend on a crop whose price is set thousands of miles away.
details.whyItMatters: The people who grow our coffee are among the most economically vulnerable. Understanding their situation is essential to building a more equitable coffee supply chain.
takeaways: Smallholders grow roughly 80 percent of global coffee
Many coffee farming families earn less than 2 dollars a day
Farmers have almost no influence over global prices

faq.question: Why are coffee farmers so vulnerable economically?
faq.answer: Farmers sell raw cherries at commodity prices but bear all production costs and climate risks. They lack storage, processing, and market access that would let them capture more value. The long supply chain between farm and cup concentrates profit at the top.

faq.question: How much of the price of a cup goes to the farmer?
faq.answer: Farmers typically receive less than 10 percent of the retail price of a cup of coffee. In some supply chains it is as low as 1 to 3 percent. The rest goes to processors, exporters, importers, roasters, and retailers.
